newsitem.title: SPAIN: Clinton seeks change in tobacco pact with US states.
newsitem.headline: Clinton seeks change in tobacco pact with US states.

text.p: U.S. President Bill Clinton said on Wednesday that a key part of the landmark accord between the tobacco industry and U.S. states would impose an "unreasonable restriction" on regulation of tobacco and ought to be changed.

Speaking at a news conference in Madrid after the NATO summit, Clinton said there were many good things in the agreement but he was concerned about the part of the agreement dealing with Food and Drug Administration regulation of tobacco.
"It seems to me to be a totally unreasonable restriction," Clinton said in response to a question.

"I have reached only one conclusion about the settlement in terms of what has to be changed, that portion that restricts the jurisdiction of the FDA in terms of limiting tobacco content in cigarettes or banning it outright ... nicotine content ... or banning it outright, because of some black market that might be created," Clinton said.
"I do think that is a change that ought to be made and I cannot believe the tobacco companies would bring down the entire settlement over that," he said.

The agreement between states and tobacco companies says that the FDA could not ban nicotine in cigarettes for a number of years and would have to show that this would not create a black market in cigarettes that contain nicotine.
Critics of the accord have said this would set impossibly tough standards for the FDA in regulating nicotine.

Under the agreement reached last month between the industry and 40 states suing it, tobacco companies would pay out $368 billion over 25 years. Some of that money would fund public health anti-smoking initiatives.

During months of tough negotiations, the tobacco companies insisted that the FDA meet certain standards before being allowed to reduce nicotine in cigarettes, including complying with a requirement that it prove such a move would not create a black market in stronger cigarettes.
Tobacco companies executives last week met with White House advisers and were not enthusiastic about reopening negotiations on the settlement, but they also did not rule out further concessions.

Clinton has created a special administration task force to review the massive agreement. Lead by Secretary of Health and Human Services Donna Shalala and White House Domestic Policy adviser Bruce Reed, the review is not yet complete.

A team of prominent public health experts and anti-smoking activists led by former U.S. Surgeon General C. Everett Koop and former Food and Drug Administration chief David Kessler were to present the White House with a critical assessment of the accord.

The Koop-Kessler criticisms are likely to carry weight in the White House, which is conducting a 30-day review of the proposed settlement, and in Congress, which would have to approve legislation to enact a deal.
